pages.name: A turning coil
pages.task: A coil turns steadily between two magnet poles. Where in its turn is its emf biggest?
pages.answer: Edge-on, with the flux changing fastest
pages.why: Edge-on, no flux passes through it, but the flux is changing fastest. The emf follows the change, not the amount. Now nothing turns. The flux itself will grow and shrink.

Edge-on, with the flux changing fastest

pages.name: Move the flux
pages.text: Two coils share one iron core, with no wire between them. The meter on the secondary reads only while the primary's current is changing. With the current held at 2 A and 5 mWb in the core, it reads zero.
pages.alt: Two coils on one iron ring, with no wire between them. The flux in the core is steady, so the meter on the secondary reads zero. Below, the flux trace and the meter trace run against time.

pages.name: Hold it still
pages.task: The primary's current rises from 0 to 2 A in 1 s, and the meter reads 0.5 V while it rises. Then the current is held at 2 A. What does the meter read now?
pages.why: Held at 2 A, the flux sits steady at 5 mWb. It is not changing at all, so no turn gets an emf. A strong field alone makes no voltage.
pages.alt: Two coils on one iron ring, with no wire between them. The flux in the core is steady, so the meter on the secondary reads zero. Below, the flux trace and the meter trace run against time.

pages.name: Against the change
pages.text: With the lamp's switch closed, the secondary's own field pushes against the change. It points against a rising flux, and with a falling one.
pages.alt: Two coils on one iron ring, with no wire between them. The flux in the core is shrinking, so the meter on the secondary reads. The lamp lights, and its current's field points with the main flux, holding it up. Below, the flux trace and the meter trace run against time.

pages.name: A falling flux
pages.task: The lamp's switch is closed. The primary's current is falling. The main flux still points up the core, but it is shrinking. Which way does the secondary's own field point?
pages.answer: Up, the same way as the main flux
pages.why: The secondary's current pushes against the change, and here the change is a fall. So its own field points up, with the main flux, to hold it up. Against the change is not always against the field.
pages.alt: Two coils on one iron ring, with no wire between them. The flux in the core is shrinking, so the meter on the secondary reads. The lamp lights, and its current's field points with the main flux, holding it up. Below, the flux trace and the meter trace run against time.
options: Up, the same way as the main flux
Nowhere: a falling flux makes no field

pages.name: Switch to AC
pages.text: On AC the emf wave follows the flux wave's slope. It peaks as the flux crosses zero. The lower trace now shows the primary's own emf. At 60 Hz, 300 turns and a peak flux of 5.5 mWb, E = 4.44 × 60 × 300 × 0.0055 = 440 V.
pages.alt: On AC the flux in the core swings as a sine, and the emf trace follows its slope, peaking as the flux crosses zero. Below, the flux trace and the emf trace run against time.

pages.name: Volts from flux
pages.task: A coil of 200 turns sits on a core whose flux peaks at 4 mWb, at 50 Hz. What rms emf does it give?
pages.why: 4.44 × 50 × 200 × 0.004 = 177.6, so 178 V rms. The peak is √2 times that, 251 V.
pages.alt: On AC the flux in the core swings as a sine, and the emf trace follows its slope, peaking as the flux crosses zero. Below, the flux trace and the emf trace run against time.

pages.name: Fix the voltage
pages.text: With the supply held at 440 V, f and N set the flux. At 60 Hz, 300 turns hold 5.5 mWb and 330 turns hold 5.0 mWb. At 50 Hz, 300 turns hold 6.6 mWb.
pages.alt: On AC the flux in the core swings as a sine, and the emf trace follows its slope, peaking as the flux crosses zero. The supply is fixed, so the flux swings just far enough to match it. Below, the flux trace and the emf trace run against time.

pages.name: More turns
pages.task: A primary on a fixed 440 V, 60 Hz supply has 300 turns and a peak flux of 5.5 mWb. It is rewound with 360 turns. What is the peak flux now?
pages.why: 440 ÷ (4.44 × 60 × 360) = 0.0046 Wb, which is 4.6 mWb. The 440 V is shared over more turns. Each turn needs less emf, so the flux swings less.
pages.alt: On AC the flux in the core swings as a sine, and the emf trace follows its slope, peaking as the flux crosses zero. The supply is fixed, so the flux swings just far enough to match it. Below, the flux trace and the emf trace run against time.

pages.name: Switch to DC
pages.text: On 24 V DC the current settles at 48 A. Only the winding's 0.5 Ω holds it back. The flux is steady, so the secondary's meter reads zero.
pages.alt: On DC the primary's current has settled far past its AC peak, and the core is saturated. The flux is steady, so the meter reads zero. Below, the flux trace and the meter trace run against time.

pages.name: Steady current
pages.task: A primary winding has a resistance of 0.4 Ω. It is put across 24 V DC. What steady current flows?
pages.why: 24 ÷ 0.4 = 60 A. The flux is steady, so the winding makes no emf to oppose the supply. On AC that emf would hold the current far lower.
pages.alt: On DC the primary's current has settled far past its AC peak, and the core is saturated. The flux is steady, so the meter reads zero. Below, the flux trace and the meter trace run against time.

pages.name: A steady rise
pages.task: The flux through a 100-turn secondary rises steadily by 3 mWb in 0.5 s. What emf does it give?
pages.why: The flux changes at 0.003 ÷ 0.5 = 0.006 Wb each second. Each turn gets 0.006 V, and 100 turns add up to 0.6 V. A steady rise gives a steady emf.
pages.alt: Two coils on one iron ring, with no wire between them. The flux in the core is growing, so the meter on the secondary reads. Below, the flux trace and the meter trace run against time.

pages.name: A lower frequency
pages.task: The 300-turn primary is built for 440 V at 60 Hz. It is put on 440 V at 40 Hz. What is its peak flux now?
pages.why: 440 ÷ (4.44 × 40 × 300) = 0.0083 Wb, which is 8.3 mWb. Each half cycle lasts longer. So the flux must swing further to make the same volts. That is 50% more flux, pushing the core towards its knee.
pages.alt: On AC the flux in the core swings as a sine, and the emf trace follows its slope, peaking as the flux crosses zero. The supply is fixed, so the flux swings just far enough to match it. Below, the flux trace and the emf trace run against time.
